Gold. A dense, soft, malleable transition metal with a distinctive bright yellow colour. It's one of the least reactive elements, resistant to most acids and atmospheric gases, which means it persists in nature in its pure, uncombined form. Because of its rarity, how easily it can be worked, and its resistance to corrosion, it has served as the primary standard for currency, jewelry, and art throughout human history.

Gold dissolves in aqua regia, a mixture of concentrated nitric and hydrochloric acid that converts it into soluble tetrachloroauric acid. Miners extract gold using gold cyanidation, also called the Elsner reaction, which uses aqueous cyanide in the presence of oxygen to leach gold from low-grade ore. Gold shows significant relativistic effects: the 6s electron orbital contracts and its energy lowers, which explains both the yellow colour from absorbing blue light and the chemical inertness. In 1909, Ernest Rutherford used gold foil in his famous experiment scattering alpha particles, revealing the dense atomic nucleus at the heart of matter. Gold forms amalgams easily with mercury, a property miners historically exploited in gold panning and mining to collect fine gold particles. Gold shares Group 11 with copper, another highly conductive and malleable metal. Mercury readily dissolves gold to form amalgams, which can be heated to distill away the mercury and recover pure gold. Uranium is often found alongside gold in ancient quartz-pebble conglomerate deposits, such as those in the Witwatersrand basin in South Africa.
